## How to measure a project

### Measure twice, in feet

Every calculator on this site works in feet and inches. Measure the longest side first, then the other side, and write both down before you start typing. For a room, measure each wall at floor level — walls are rarely as square as they look, so take the biggest number if the two ends differ.

### Depth matters as much as area

A patio is not just 10 by 10 feet — it is 10 by 10 feet at 4 inches thick . The same area at 6 inches takes half as much material again. The calculators ask for depth wherever it matters: concrete thickness, mulch depth, topsoil depth.

### Always add a little extra

Every calculator here adds a waste allowance by default — usually 10%. It covers spillage, uneven ground, cut-offs and the odd mistake. Running out halfway through a pour or a paint job costs far more than one extra bag or gallon.

### When the numbers get big, call a truck

Once a concrete job passes about one cubic yard — 45 bags of 80 lb mix — ready-mix delivered by truck is usually cheaper and far less work than mixing bags by hand. The concrete calculator tells you when you have crossed that line.

These calculators are estimates for planning only. They are not professional advice, and a supplier's own figures win over anything here. Confirm quantities with your supplier before you order, and check your local building code before you build anything structural.

For a slab, multiply length by width by thickness — then divide by 27 to get cubic yards. For fence post holes, work out one hole and multiply. The calculator does both, and tells you how many bags to buy.

## How the maths works

### Slabs: length × width × thickness, divided by 27

A cubic yard is 27 cubic feet — a cube 3 feet on every side. So a slab 10 feet by 10 feet at 4 inches thick is 10 × 10 × (4 ÷ 12) = 33.33 cubic feet, and 33.33 ÷ 27 = 1.23 cubic yards. The 10% waste allowance takes it to 1.36 cubic yards.

### Bags: divide by what one bag makes

Bag yields are printed on the bag and are the same across the big brands: an 80 lb bag makes 0.60 cubic feet (45 bags per yard), a 60 lb bag makes 0.45 cubic feet (60 per yard), and a 40 lb bag makes 0.30 cubic feet (90 per yard). So 36.67 cubic feet ÷ 0.60 = 61.1 — we round up to 62 bags.

### Post holes: the cylinder formula

A round hole is a cylinder: π × radius² × depth. A 12-inch hole, 24 inches deep, is π × 0.5² × 2 = 1.57 cubic feet. That is 3 bags of 80 lb mix per hole. The fence calculator works out the concrete for a whole fence line at once.

### Common slab sizes

Slab | Cubic yards (+10%) | 80 lb bags | 

10 × 10 ft at 4 in | 1.36 | 62 | 

12 × 12 ft at 4 in | 1.96 | 89 | 

10 × 20 ft at 4 in | 2.72 | 123 | 

20 × 30 ft driveway at 6 in | 12.22 | 550 | 

## Types of concrete — and the temperatures they work in

Not all bagged concrete is the same. The mix you pick decides how fast it sets and how strong it ends up.

Type | Best for | Temperature notes | 

General-purpose mix | Slabs, footings, driveways | The standard all-rounder. Works from 50 to 90°F. | 

Fast-setting mix | Fence posts, small repairs | Sets in 20 to 40 minutes. Above 85°F it can set in under 10 minutes — work fast, or wait for a cool day. | 

High-strength mix (5,000 PSI) | Driveways, heavy loads | Same temperature range, but needs a full 28 days to reach full strength — longer in the cold. | 

Ready-mix (by truck) | Anything over about half a cubic yard | The plant adjusts the mix for hot or cold weather. The cheapest way to pour big. | 

 Temperature matters more than the bag. The sweet spot is 50 to 90°F (10 to 32°C), ideally 65 to 75°F. Below 40°F the chemical reaction slows right down, and if fresh concrete freezes before it has gained strength it can be permanently damaged — keep it above 50°F for the first week, with blankets if you have to. Above 90°F it sets too fast, gets hard to work, and loses strength; above 95°F it is outside the industry standard (ACI 305) and should not be poured. Hot day? Pour early in the morning, keep the mix shaded, and have everything ready before the truck arrives.

## Mixing concrete at home — in a wheelbarrow

For small jobs, a wheelbarrow and a hoe beat renting a mixer. One to three 80 lb bags per batch is the working limit — a full 6 cubic foot barrow could hold more, but three bags of wet mix already weigh about 250 lb.

 - Mix where you pour. A loaded barrow is too heavy to push far.

 - Measure the water. About 3 quarts (0.75 gallons) per 80 lb bag. Pour about two-thirds of it into the barrow first.

 - Add the dry mix. Tip the bag in rather than shaking it, to keep the dust down.

 - Chop and fold with a hoe for 3 to 5 minutes until the colour is even and there are no dry pockets hiding in the corners.

 - Add the last water a little at a time. Stop when a squeezed handful holds its shape. One extra quart in an 80 lb bag can cost up to 40% of the strength.

 - Place it straight away. Do not add water once it starts to stiffen. Rinse the barrow before the mix sets.

Wet concrete burns skin — wear gloves and eye protection, and wash off any splashes right away.

## Common questions

### How much concrete do I need for a 10×10 slab?

1.36 cubic yards with the 10% waste allowance, or 62 bags of 80 lb mix.

### How many 80 lb bags of concrete are in a cubic yard?

45 bags.

### Can I pour concrete when it is cold?

Below 40°F the chemical reaction slows right down, and fresh concrete can be permanently damaged if it freezes. Do not pour on frozen ground, and keep the concrete above 50°F for the first week.

Figures verified November 2026 against Quikrete's published bag yields and several concrete calculators. Yields vary slightly by brand — check the bag. This page is an estimate for planning only, not engineering advice; structural pours and anything governed by building codes should be sized by a qualified professional.


## Paint Calculator — How Many Gallons of Paint Do I Need? (https://builditcalculators.com/paint.html)

Paint calculator

# How many gallons of paint do I need?

Measure the walls, subtract the doors and windows, multiply by the number of coats, and divide by what one gallon covers. One gallon covers about 350 square feet per coat on a smooth wall.

### Worked example — see the maths

 A 12 by 12 foot room, 8 foot ceilings 
 Walls: 2 × (12 + 12) × 8 = 384 sq ft 
 Minus 1 door and 2 windows 
 384 − 21 − 30 = 333 sq ft to paint 
 Two coats 
 333 × 2 = 666 sq ft of painting 
 At 350 sq ft per gallon 
 666 ÷ 350 = 1.90 gallons 
 Buy 
 2 gallons 
 With the ceiling too 
 477 sq ft to paint — 2.73 gallons, buy 3 

## How the maths works

### Wall area is perimeter times height

Walk around the room and add up the wall lengths — that is the perimeter. Multiply by the ceiling height and you have the wall area. A 12 by 12 foot room has a 48 foot perimeter; at 8 feet high that is 384 square feet of wall.

### Subtract what you do not paint

Doors and windows are not painted, so take them off: a standard door is 21 square feet, a typical window is 15. It is a small correction, but on a room with three windows it saves you nearly half a gallon.

### One gallon covers about 350 square feet per coat

That is the safe planning number for smooth, previously painted drywall. The label may say 400, but that assumes perfect conditions and a professional roller. Textured walls take more — plan for 250 to 300 square feet per gallon — and bare drywall drinks paint, so prime it first.

### Two coats, not one

Almost every interior job needs two coats for an even color. The only exception is repainting the same color on paint that is already in good shape. Buy the second coat now — matching the color later is harder than it sounds.

## Paint grades — what the extra money buys

Paint comes in three quality grades, and the price gap is bigger than it looks. The dearer paint usually covers better, so it needs fewer coats — which is where it pays for itself.

Grade | Price per gallon | Coverage | Lasts | Best for | 

Contractor / economy | $15–$28 | 200–300 sq ft | 2–4 years | Rentals, quick flips | 

Mid-grade | $28–$45 | 350–400 sq ft | 5–10 years | Most homes | 

Premium | $45–$80 | 400+ sq ft | 10–15+ years | A home you plan to stay in | 

The difference is what is in the can: premium paint has more titanium dioxide (the white pigment that hides the old colour) and better acrylic binders, so it usually covers in two coats where economy paint takes three or four. On a whole house that can make the dearer paint cheaper per job, not dearer.

### Water-based or oil-based?

For about 95% of jobs, water-based latex paint is the right choice — it dries fast, has little smell, and cleans up with soap and water. Look for 100% acrylic on the label for exterior work: it flexes with temperature changes and resists moisture and sun. Oil-based (alkyd) paint is now mostly for trim, cabinets and metal, where its hard finish earns its keep — it smells strong, dries slowly and needs solvents to clean up.

### Finishes, from flat to gloss

Flat hides wall bumps best but marks easily and is hard to wash — good for ceilings and low-traffic rooms. Eggshell and satin are the middle ground: washable enough for living rooms, kitchens and hallways. Semi-gloss and high-gloss are the toughest and easiest to clean, so they suit doors, trim and bathrooms — but their shine shows every bump, so the surface underneath has to be smooth.

## Common questions

### How much paint do I need for a 12×12 room?

The walls are 384 square feet, and one gallon covers about 350 square feet per coat — so about 2¼ gallons for two coats. Buy 3 gallons to be safe.

### How many coats of paint do I need?

Two, for almost every interior job. One coat rarely covers evenly.

### Is expensive paint worth it?

Usually yes. Premium paint covers in two coats where economy paint takes three or four, and lasts 10–15 years instead of 2–4.

Figures verified November 2026 against manufacturer data sheets (Benjamin Moore, Sherwin-Williams, Behr) and several paint calculators. Coverage varies by brand, surface and color — the number on your can wins. This page is an estimate for planning only.

# How much mulch do I need?

Multiply your bed's area by the depth, and you have the volume. One cubic yard covers 108 square feet at 3 inches deep — the standard depth for a planting bed.

 A 10 by 20 foot bed, 3 inches deep

## How the maths works

### Cubic yards = area × depth ÷ 324

That is the shortcut from the Texas A&M AgriLife Extension: square feet times depth in inches, divided by 324, gives cubic yards. It works because one cubic yard is 27 cubic feet, and 27 × 12 = 324.

### How deep should mulch be?

Two to three inches is right for most flower and shrub beds — enough to hold moisture and block weeds, thin enough that the soil underneath can still breathe. Four inches is for a deep barrier around trees. More than 4 inches can suffocate roots, so do not overdo it.

### Bags or bulk?

One cubic yard is 13.5 bags of 2 cubic feet. For a small bed, bags are easy to carry and store. For anything over about 2 cubic yards, bulk delivery is usually much cheaper per yard — and far less plastic to throw away.

## Types of mulch — which one for your climate

Mulch comes in two families. Organic mulch is made from things that were once alive — bark, wood chips, straw, shredded leaves, compost, pine needles. It breaks down over time and feeds the soil, but you have to top it up every year or two. Inorganic mulch never breaks down — gravel, river rock, rubber chips, landscape fabric. It lasts for years but feeds the soil nothing.

Most of the bagged mulch in a garden centre is shredded bark or wood — usually pine, cedar or hardwood bark.

Climate | Best pick | Why | 

Hot and dry | Light-coloured bark or straw, 3 to 4 in deep | Holds moisture and keeps roots cool. Gravel can get hot enough to scorch roots. | 

Wet and humid | Coarse bark nuggets | Lets air through. Fine mulch stays soggy and breeds mould and slugs. | 

Cold winters | Thick straw or coarse wood chips | Insulates roots and stops the soil heaving as it freezes and thaws. | 

Windy or steep slopes | Heavy wood chips, or gravel | Light straw just blows away. | 

Whatever the climate, keep mulch 2 to 3 inches deep and an inch or two away from plant stems — piled against a trunk it holds moisture and rots the bark.

## Common questions

### How much mulch do I need for a 100 sq ft bed?

At 3 inches deep, about 0.93 cubic yards — around 13 bags of 2 cubic feet.

### How deep should mulch be?

Two to three inches for most flower and shrub beds, four inches around trees. More than 4 inches can suffocate roots.

### What mulch is best for a hot, dry garden?

Light-coloured bark or straw, 3 to 4 inches deep. It holds moisture and keeps roots cool; gravel can get hot enough to scorch roots.

Figures verified November 2026 against Texas A&M AgriLife Extension and several mulch calculators. Bag sizes and coverage vary by brand — check the label. This page is an estimate for planning only.


## Topsoil Calculator & Gravel Calculator — Yards, Tons & Bags (https://builditcalculators.com/topsoil.html)

Topsoil & gravel calculator

# How much topsoil or gravel do I need?

Same maths as mulch — area times depth — but these materials are sold by weight too, so the calculator gives you cubic yards and tons. A yard of topsoil weighs about a ton; a yard of gravel weighs about 1.4 tons.

### Worked example — see the maths

 A 10 by 10 foot area, 6 inches deep 
 100 sq ft × 6 in ÷ 324 = 1.85 cubic yards (50 cubic feet) 
 As topsoil 
 1.85 × 2,000 lb = 3,704 lb — 1.85 tons 
 As gravel 
 1.85 × 2,800 lb = 5,185 lb — 2.59 tons 
 As sand 
 1.85 × 2,700 lb = 5,000 lb — 2.50 tons 
 Watch your truck 
 A yard of gravel weighs about 2,800 lb — more than many half-ton pickups are rated to carry in one load 

## How the maths works

### Volume first, weight second

Volume is the same for every material: area in square feet times depth in inches, divided by 324, gives cubic yards. Then weight is cubic yards times the material's weight per yard. That is where materials differ — a yard of mulch weighs about 500 lb, a yard of gravel about 2,800 lb.

### Weight per cubic yard (dry, planning figures)

Material | Pounds per yard | Tons per yard | 

Topsoil | about 2,000 | 1.00 | 

Gravel / crushed stone | about 2,800 | 1.40 | 

Sand (dry) | about 2,700 | 1.35 | 

Mulch | about 500 | 0.25 | 

Wet material weighs more — wet topsoil can reach 2,800 to 3,200 lb per yard. If you are ordering by the ton or hauling it yourself, ask your supplier what their material weighs. Their scale ticket wins over any calculator.

### How deep?

Six inches of topsoil is a good depth for a new lawn or a garden bed. For top-dressing an existing lawn, 1 to 2 inches is enough. For a gravel driveway or path, 3 to 4 inches of compacted gravel holds up well.

## Three grades of gravel — and what each costs

Gravel is sold by the ton, and the grade decides both the price and the job it suits. Prices are per ton delivered, typical US prices for 2026 — they vary a lot by region, and delivery often adds $50 to $150 a trip.

Grade | Size | Best for | Price per ton | 

Crusher run / road base (#21A) | ¾ in down to dust | Driveway base — the fines compact into a hard surface | $20–$40 | 

#57 crushed stone | ¾ in, angular edges | Drainage, driveways, concrete mix | $25–$50 | 

Pea gravel | ⅜ in, rounded | Paths, patios, decoration — smooth underfoot | $30–$60 | 

Crusher run is the cheapest because it is just crushed rock with the dust left in — and that dust is exactly what makes it lock together. Pea gravel costs the most because it is screened, washed and rounded. Do not use pea gravel for a driveway: the round stones never lock together, so they shift under tires. One ton is roughly 0.7 cubic yards, so the calculator's cubic yards times 1.4 gives you the tons to order.

## Types of topsoil — and which plants each suits

"Topsoil" on a delivery ticket can mean several different soils. What it is made of decides what will grow well in it.

Soil type | What it is like | Best plants | 

Loam | A balanced mix of sand, silt and clay — the gardener's favourite | Almost everything: most vegetables, lawns, roses, shrubs | 

Sandy | Drains fast, warms up early, low in nutrients | Carrots, radishes, potatoes, rosemary, thyme, lavender | 

Clay | Heavy and sticky, rich in nutrients, holds water | Cabbage, broccoli, kale, beans, roses, hydrangeas | 

Silty | Smooth and fertile, holds moisture well | Tomatoes, peppers, leafy greens, peonies, hostas | 

Peaty (acidic) | Dark, spongy, low pH (4.5–5.5) | Blueberries, rhododendrons, azaleas, camellias, heather | 

Chalky (alkaline) | Pale, free-draining, high pH (7.5–8.5) | Lavender, clematis, lilac, spinach, cabbage, kale | 

If you are buying topsoil for a vegetable garden, ask for screened loam with compost mixed in — that is the safest all-rounder. And if you want blueberries, do not plant them in ordinary topsoil: they need acidic soil, and in heavy clay they will barely fruit. Mix in peat or use an ericaceous (acid-loving) compost instead.

## Common questions

### How many tons of gravel are in a cubic yard?

About 1.4 tons.

### Which gravel is cheapest?

Crusher run (road base), about $20–$40 a ton delivered. Pea gravel costs the most, about $30–$60 a ton.

### What soil is best for vegetables?

Screened loam with compost mixed in. Blueberries are the exception — they need acidic soil, not ordinary topsoil.

Figures verified November 2026 against The Calculator Site, US Army FM 5-434 material weights and several yard calculators. Weights are dry planning figures and vary with moisture and compaction. This page is an estimate for planning only.


## Tile Calculator — How Many Floor Tiles & Boxes Do I Need? (https://builditcalculators.com/tile.html)

Tile calculator

# How many floor tiles do I need?

Divide your floor area by one tile's area, then add 10% for cuts and breakage. A 10 by 12 foot room takes 120 twelve-inch tiles — 132 with waste — which is 14 boxes of 10.

## How the maths works

### One tile's area, then divide

A 12 by 12 inch tile covers 1 square foot. A 12 by 24 inch tile covers 2. Divide your floor area by one tile's area and you have the tile count before waste. The calculator does the inches-to-feet conversion for you — just type the tile size in inches.

### Always add waste

Tiles get cut at the edges, around door frames and around pipes, and a few always break. Ten percent is the standard allowance for straight rows. Go to 15% for diagonal patterns, herringbone, or rooms with lots of corners and angles.

### Buy a spare box

Tile dye lots change between batches, and a box from a different lot can look slightly off. Buying one spare box now — same lot, same color — is far easier than hunting for a match in two years when one tile cracks.

## Common questions

### How many tiles do I need?

Divide the floor area by one tile's area — a 12×12 inch tile covers 1 square foot — then add 10% waste.

### How much extra tile should I buy?

10% for straight rows, 15% for diagonal patterns, herringbone, or rooms with lots of corners.

### Should I buy a spare box of tile?

Yes. Tile dye lots change between batches, and a matching box is hard to find later when one tile cracks.

Figures verified November 2026. Tile coverage varies by brand and by grout joint width — the box label wins. This page is an estimate for planning only.


## Flooring Calculator — How Much Laminate, Vinyl Plank & Hardwood Flooring Do I Need? (https://builditcalculators.com/flooring.html)

# How much flooring do I need?

Measure the room, pick the flooring, and the calculator tells you how many square feet to order and how many boxes to buy. A 12 by 15 foot room takes 198 square feet with 10% waste — 10 boxes of laminate at 20 square feet a box.

 A 12 by 15 foot room

 198 sq ft to order 
 Laminate, 20 sq ft per box

 Vinyl plank, 24 sq ft per box

## How the maths works

### Area, then add waste

Room area is length times width. Add 10% for a straight lay — it covers the cuts at the walls, a plank or two that arrives damaged, and the odd mistake. Go to 15% for diagonal layouts or rooms with lots of corners and closets, and 20% for herringbone or chevron.

### Boxes: divide and round up

Flooring is sold by the box, not by the square foot, so divide what you need to order by the coverage on the box and round up. Coverage varies by brand — laminate is usually about 20 square feet a box, vinyl plank about 24, hardwood about 20 — so check the label and type the exact number in.

### Underlayment and acclimation

Laminate and floating hardwood need underlayment between the planks and the subfloor — it softens footsteps and blocks moisture. Rolls usually cover 100 square feet. Vinyl plank with an attached pad often needs none. Let wood flooring sit in the room for at least 48 hours before you lay it — solid hardwood up to 7 days — so it adjusts to your home's temperature and humidity.

## Common questions

### How much flooring do I need for a 12x12 room?

144 square feet, and 159 with 10% waste — 8 boxes of laminate at 20 square feet a box.

### How much extra flooring should I buy?

10% for a straight lay in a rectangular room. Use 15% for diagonal layouts or rooms with lots of corners, and 20% for herringbone.

### How many square feet are in a box of flooring?

It varies by brand — laminate is usually about 20, vinyl plank about 24, hardwood about 20, and engineered hardwood about 22. The exact number is printed on the box.

Figures verified November 2026. Box coverage varies by brand — the label wins. This page is an estimate for planning only.

## How the maths works

### Sheets: area divided by 32, plus waste

Wall area is the room's perimeter times its height, minus doors and windows. Add the ceiling if you are boarding it too. Divide by the sheet size — 32 square feet for a 4 by 8 — and add 10% for cuts around outlets, corners and angles.

### Finishing materials come per sheet

The estimating guides from the gypsum manufacturers work out to about the same numbers on every calculator: 32 screws per wall sheet (about one per square foot), 1 gallon of joint compound per 100 square feet for a three-coat finish, and 0.37 feet of paper tape per square foot of board. Ceilings take about half again as many screws as walls, because gravity is working against the board.

### One pound of screws goes a long way

A 1 lb box of 1¼ inch drywall screws holds roughly 200 screws — about 6 sheets' worth. A 5 lb box covers about 30 sheets. Buy screws by the box, not by the handful.

## Common questions

### How many drywall sheets do I need for a room?

Take the wall area (perimeter times height, minus doors and windows), divide by 32 square feet per 4×8 sheet, and add 10% for cuts.

### How many screws per sheet of drywall?

About 32 per wall sheet. Ceilings take about half again as many, because gravity works against the board.

### How much joint compound do I need?

About 1 gallon per 100 square feet for a three-coat finish.

Figures verified November 2026 against USG's installation guide, the Gypsum Construction Handbook and several drywall calculators. Actual amounts vary with framing spacing and finish level — confirm with your supplier. This page is an estimate for planning only.


## Fence Calculator — Posts, Pickets, Rails & Concrete (https://builditcalculators.com/fence.html)

Fence calculator

# How much fencing do I need?

Posts every 8 feet, pickets 5.5 inches wide, 2 to 3 rails per section, and one bag of concrete per post. Type in your fence length and height and get the whole materials list.

## Your fence

Fill in your numbers — the answer updates as you type.

 Fence length (feet) 

 Fence height (feet) 

 Check your local height limit — 6 feet is the usual maximum for a backyard fence. 

 Post spacing

 6 ft — stronger, for wind or heavy boards 

 8 feet matches 8 ft rail stock exactly, so there is no cutting waste.

 1×6 pickets (actually 5.5 in wide) 
 1×4 pickets (actually 3.5 in wide)

 0 for a solid privacy fence; about 2.5 inches for a classic spaced picket look.

### Worked example — see the maths

 100 feet of 6 foot privacy fence, 8 ft post spacing 
 13 sections — and 14 posts (sections plus one for the end) 
 Pickets, 5.5 in wide, no gap, 10% waste 
 241 pickets (2.2 per foot before waste) 
 Rails (3 per section for a 6 ft fence) 
 39 rails — 8 ft 2×4s 
 Concrete (one 80 lb bag per post) 
 14 bags 
 Same fence at 6 ft spacing 
 17 sections, 18 posts — four extra holes, but a fence that handles wind better 

## How the maths works

### Posts: length divided by spacing, plus one

Eight feet on center is the standard — it matches 8 foot rail stock with no waste, and it is the practical maximum for a wood fence. Drop to 6 feet in exposed positions, with heavy solid boards, or on soft ground. Whatever the spacing, add one post at the end: it is the post everyone forgets.

### Pickets: 2.2 per foot, not 2

This is the mistake that leaves people short. A nominal 1×6 picket is actually 5.5 inches wide, so 12 ÷ 5.5 = 2.2 pickets per foot. Dividing by 6 inches instead gives 200 pickets for a 100 foot fence — 19 short of the 219 you actually need.

### Rails: 2, 3 or 4 per section

Fences under 5 feet tall need 2 rails per section. Five to 7 feet — the common 6 foot privacy fence — needs 3. An 8 foot fence needs 4, and 6×6 posts instead of 4×4.

### Concrete: one bag per post

For a 4×4 post in a 10 to 12 inch hole, 24 inches deep, one 80 lb bag is the usual rule. Use the concrete calculator if your holes are a different size — it works out post holes exactly.

## Common questions

### How many fence posts do I need?

Divide the fence length by the post spacing — usually 8 feet — then add one post at the end.

### How many pickets do I need for a 100 ft fence?

219, with 1×6 pickets. They are really 5.5 inches wide, so it is 2.2 pickets per foot, not 2.

### How much concrete per fence post?

One 80 lb bag, for a 4×4 post in a 10 to 12 inch hole, 24 inches deep.

Figures verified November 2026 against several fence calculators and lumber guides. Post depth should be at least a third of the post's height and below your local frost line. Check your property line and local rules before you dig — call 811 first. This page is an estimate for planning only.


## Deck Calculator — Decking Boards, Joists & Screws (https://builditcalculators.com/deck.html)

Deck calculator

# How much decking do I need?

A 5.5 inch wide deck board covers about 5⅝ inches of deck once you leave a small gap — so one square foot of deck takes about 2.13 linear feet of board. A 12 by 16 foot deck needs about 410 linear feet of decking.

## Your deck

Fill in your numbers — the answer updates as you type.

 Deck length (feet) 

 Deck width (feet) 

 Deck board width 

 5/4×6 boards (actually 5.5 in wide) 
 2×4 boards (actually 3.5 in wide) 

 Gap between boards (inches) 

 ⅛ inch is standard — it lets rain through and gives boards room to swell. 

 Joist spacing (inches) 

 16 in on center — standard 
 12 in on center — stiffer, for diagonal boards

—

 Joists

### Worked example — see the maths

 A 12 by 16 foot deck 
 192 sq ft 
 Decking, 5.5 in boards with a ⅛ in gap 
 192 × 12 ÷ 5.625 = 410 linear feet 
 Joists at 16 in on center 
 13 joists , 12 feet long each (156 linear feet) 
 Screws (about 3.5 per sq ft) 
 672 screws 
 A 10 by 10 foot deck 
 100 sq ft — 213 linear feet of decking 

## How the maths works

### Board coverage: width plus gap

Each board covers its own width plus the gap beside it. A 5.5 inch board with a ⅛ inch gap covers 5.625 inches, so one square foot of deck takes 12 ÷ 5.625 = 2.13 linear feet of board. Narrower boards take more: a 3.5 inch board with the same gap needs 3.3 linear feet per square foot.

### Joists: one every 16 inches, plus one

Joists run under the decking every 16 inches on center — that is the standard for 5/4 decking. Count them the same way as fence posts: length divided by spacing, plus one at the end. For a 16 foot deck that is 13 joists.

### Screws: two per board at every joist

Each deck board gets two screws where it crosses each joist. That works out to about 350 screws per 100 square feet of deck — 3.5 per square foot. Buy stainless or coated deck screws; ordinary screws rust and stain the wood.

### Do not forget the frame

This calculator covers decking, joists and screws. A real deck also needs beams, posts, footings, ledger board, flashing and railing. Footings and posts depend on your local frost depth and building code — check both before you build.

## Common questions

### How many deck screws do I need?

About 350 screws per 100 square feet of deck — two per board at every joist.

### How far apart should deck joists be?

16 inches on center, which is the standard for 5/4 decking.

### How many boards do I need for a deck?

It depends on board width. A 5.5 inch board with a ⅛ inch gap covers 5.625 inches, so one square foot of deck takes 2.13 linear feet of board.

Figures verified November 2026 against lumber guides and several deck calculators. Board widths are actual milled sizes, not nominal labels. This page is an estimate for planning only, not structural advice — decks are governed by local building codes.

# About Home & Garden Calculators

Eight free calculators for American homeowners — concrete, paint, mulch, topsoil and gravel, tile, drywall, fence and deck. Type in your measurements, get the answer in seconds, and see the maths so you can check it yourself.

## What this site is

Every calculator on this site answers one question: how much material do I need? We use US units — feet, inches, gallons, cubic yards, pounds — and plain English, no jargon. Every formula is shown on the page, with a worked example using real numbers, so you can follow the maths yourself.

## What it is not

It is not professional advice. The numbers are estimates for planning: good enough to order materials and budget a job, not a substitute for a contractor, an engineer, or your local building code. Prices and local rules change — confirm them with your supplier before you buy.

## How the numbers are worked out

Every formula on this site was checked against published sources in November 2026 — manufacturer data sheets (Quikrete, USG), university extension guides (Texas A&M AgriLife), the US Army's earthmoving manual, and several independent calculators. Where sources disagree, the page says so and uses the safe planning number.

## How much concrete do I need? (https://builditcalculators.com/how-much-concrete-do-i-need.html)

A 10 by 10 foot patio slab, 4 inches thick, takes 1.36 cubic yards of concrete — 62 bags of 80 lb mix. The maths is simple: multiply length by width by thickness, then divide by 27 to get cubic yards. For fence post holes, work out one hole and multiply.
### Worked example

A 10 by 10 foot patio slab, 4 inches thick 1.23 cubic yards

With 10% waste added 1.36 cubic yards

80 lb bags 62 bags

60 lb bags 82 bags

40 lb bags 123 bags

One fence post hole, 12 inches wide and 24 inches deep 3 bags of 80 lb mix

## How the maths works

### Slabs: length × width × thickness, divided by 27

A cubic yard is 27 cubic feet — a cube 3 feet on every side. So a slab 10 feet by 10 feet at 4 inches thick is 10 × 10 × (4 ÷ 12) = 33.33 cubic feet, and 33.33 ÷ 27 = 1.23 cubic yards. The 10% waste allowance takes it to 1.36 cubic yards.

### Bags: divide by what one bag makes

Bag yields are printed on the bag and are the same across the big brands: an 80 lb bag makes 0.60 cubic feet (45 bags per yard), a 60 lb bag makes 0.45 cubic feet (60 per yard), and a 40 lb bag makes 0.30 cubic feet (90 per yard). So 36.67 cubic feet ÷ 0.60 = 61.1 — we round up to 62 bags.

### Post holes: the cylinder formula

A round hole is a cylinder: π × radius² × depth. A 12-inch hole, 24 inches deep, is π × 0.5² × 2 = 1.57 cubic feet. That is 3 bags of 80 lb mix per hole. The fence calculator works out the concrete for a whole fence line at once.

### Common slab sizes

 | Slab   | Cubic yards (+10%)   | 80 lb bags

 | 10 × 10 ft at 4 in   | 1.36   | 62

 | 12 × 12 ft at 4 in   | 1.96   | 89

 | 10 × 20 ft at 4 in   | 2.72   | 123

 | 20 × 30 ft driveway at 6 in   | 12.22   | 550

## Bags or ready-mix?

Once a job passes about one cubic yard — 45 bags of 80 lb mix — ready-mix delivered by truck is usually cheaper and far less work than mixing bags by hand. Bags make sense for small pours and post holes; anything bigger, call the truck.

## Pouring temperatures

Concrete pours best between 50 and 90°F. Below 40°F it sets very slowly and can be permanently damaged if it freezes; above 95°F it sets too fast, loses strength, and is outside the industry standard. The concrete calculator page has the full guide to concrete types and pouring temperatures.

## Common questions

### How much concrete do I need for a 10×10 slab?

1.36 cubic yards with the 10% waste allowance, or 62 bags of 80 lb mix.

### How many 80 lb bags of concrete are in a cubic yard?

45 bags.

### How much concrete do I need for one fence post hole?

3 bags of 80 lb mix, for a hole 12 inches wide and 24 inches deep.

### When should I order ready-mix instead of bags?

Once a job passes about one cubic yard — 45 bags of 80 lb mix. Ready-mix delivered by truck is usually cheaper and far less work than mixing that many bags by hand.

Figures verified November 2026 against Quikrete's published bag yields and several concrete calculators. Yields vary slightly by brand — check the bag. This page is an estimate for planning only, not engineering advice; structural pours and anything governed by building codes should be sized by a qualified professional.

## How many deck boards do I need? (https://builditcalculators.com/how-many-deck-boards-do-i-need.html)

A 12 by 16 foot deck takes about 410 linear feet of 5.5 inch decking — roughly 2.13 linear feet of board for every square foot of deck. Add joists at 16 inches on center and about 350 screws per 100 square feet, and you have the whole shopping list.
### Worked example

A 12 by 16 foot deck 192 sq ft

Decking, 5.5 in boards 410 linear feet

Joists at 16 in on center 13 joists

Screws 672 screws

A 10 by 10 foot deck 213 linear feet of decking

## How the maths works

### Decking boards: 2.13 linear feet per square foot

A 5.5 inch board with a ⅛ inch gap covers 5.625 inches, so one square foot of deck takes 2.13 linear feet of board. Multiply your deck area by 2.13 to get the linear feet, then round up — and buy a couple of spare boards for cuts, because a board cut wrong is the most common waste on a deck.

### Joists: 16 inches on center

Joists run under the decking, 16 inches apart. Divide the deck's length by 16 inches and add one joist for the end. A 12 by 16 foot deck has 13 joists.

### Screws: two per board at every joist

Count about 350 screws per 100 square feet of deck — two screws where each board crosses each joist. A 12 by 16 foot deck takes 672 screws.

### Common deck sizes

 | Deck   | Area   | Decking (5.5 in boards)

 | 10 × 10 ft   | 100 sq ft   | 213 linear feet

 | 12 × 12 ft   | 144 sq ft   | about 307 linear feet

 | 12 × 16 ft   | 192 sq ft   | 410 linear feet

 | 16 × 20 ft   | 320 sq ft   | about 682 linear feet

## What size boards?

5.5 inch wide boards (sold as 1×6) are the standard for decking. Wider boards cover faster but cup more in the sun; narrower boards look busier and use more screws. The deck calculator works with 5.5 inch boards.

## Common questions

### How many deck boards do I need for a deck?

It depends on board width. A 5.5 inch board with a ⅛ inch gap covers 5.625 inches, so one square foot of deck takes 2.13 linear feet of board.

### How far apart should deck joists be?

16 inches on center, which is the standard for 5/4 decking.

### How many deck screws do I need?

About 350 screws per 100 square feet of deck — two per board at every joist.

### How much decking do I need for a 10×10 deck?

213 linear feet of 5.5 inch decking.

Figures verified November 2026 against supplier listings and several online calculators. These are estimates for planning only — confirm quantities with your supplier before you order.

## How much drywall do I need? (https://builditcalculators.com/how-much-drywall-do-i-need.html)

A 12 by 12 foot room with 8 foot ceilings takes 17 sheets of 4×8 drywall — plus 544 screws, 5 gallons of joint compound and 176 feet of paper tape. The maths is just area: work out the wall area, add the ceiling if you are boarding it, and divide by 32 square feet per sheet.
### Worked example

A 12 by 12 foot room, 8 foot ceilings 333 sq ft

Plus the ceiling 477 sq ft of board

4 × 8 sheets, 10% waste 17 sheets

Screws 544 screws

Joint compound 5 gallons

Paper tape 176 feet

## How the maths works

### Wall area: perimeter × height, minus doors and windows

Add up all four wall lengths, multiply by the ceiling height, then subtract about 21 sq ft for each door and 15 sq ft for each window. A 12 by 12 foot room with 8 foot ceilings has 384 sq ft of wall — 333 sq ft after one door and two windows.

### Sheets: divide by 32, add 10%

A 4×8 sheet covers 32 sq ft. Divide your total area by 32 and add 10% for cuts. The 12 by 12 room needs 477 sq ft of board with the ceiling — 477 ÷ 32 = 14.9, plus 10% is 16.4, so 17 sheets.

### Screws: about 32 per sheet

Budget about 32 screws per wall sheet. Ceilings take about half again as many, because gravity works against the board.

### Joint compound and tape

Allow about 1 gallon of joint compound per 100 sq ft for a three-coat finish, and enough paper tape to cover every seam — 176 feet for the 12 by 12 room.

## Cutting waste down

Hang sheets horizontally on walls — fewer seams to tape, and the long edges land on studs. Measure twice before you cut: a sheet cut short is the most common waste on a drywall job.

## Common questions

### How many drywall sheets do I need for a room?

Take the wall area (perimeter times height, minus doors and windows), divide by 32 square feet per 4×8 sheet, and add 10% for cuts.

### How many screws per sheet of drywall?

About 32 per wall sheet. Ceilings take about half again as many, because gravity works against the board.

### How much joint compound do I need?

About 1 gallon per 100 square feet for a three-coat finish.

### How much drywall do I need for a 12×12 room?

17 sheets of 4×8 drywall with the ceiling, plus 544 screws, 5 gallons of joint compound and 176 feet of tape.

Figures verified November 2026 against supplier listings and several online calculators. These are estimates for planning only — confirm quantities with your supplier before you order.

## How many fence pickets and posts do I need? (https://builditcalculators.com/how-many-fence-pickets-and-posts-do-i-need.html)

100 feet of 6 foot privacy fence takes 14 posts, 241 pickets and 39 rails — plus 14 bags of concrete, one per post. The trick is the pickets: a 1×6 picket is really only 5.5 inches wide, so it takes 2.2 pickets per foot, not 2.
### Worked example

100 feet of 6 foot privacy fence, 8 ft post spacing 13 sections — 14 posts

Pickets, 10% waste 241 pickets

Rails 39 rails

Concrete 14 bags

Same fence at 6 ft spacing 17 sections, 18 posts

## How the maths works

### Posts: length ÷ spacing, plus one

Divide the fence length by the post spacing — usually 8 feet — then add one post at the end. 100 feet ÷ 8 = 12.5, so 13 sections and 14 posts.

### Pickets: 2.2 per foot

1×6 pickets are really 5.5 inches wide. That is 2.2 pickets per foot of fence — 219 pickets for 100 feet, 241 with 10% waste for cuts and the odd bad board.

### Rails: 3 per section

A 6 foot privacy fence needs three horizontal rails per section — top, middle and bottom. 13 sections × 3 rails = 39 rails.

### Concrete: one bag per post

One 80 lb bag sets a 4×4 post in a 10 to 12 inch hole, 24 inches deep. 14 posts means 14 bags. The concrete calculator works out post holes on their own.

### Common fence lengths

 | Fence   | Posts   | Pickets (+10%)   | Rails   | Concrete bags

 | 50 ft   | 8   | 121   | 21   | 8

 | 100 ft   | 14   | 241   | 39   | 14

 | 150 ft   | 20   | 363   | 57   | 20

## How deep should the posts go?

At least a third of the post goes underground, and below your frost line — 24 inches deep is the usual minimum for a 6 foot fence. Go deeper in cold climates, where the frost line is lower.

## Common questions

### How many fence posts do I need?

Divide the fence length by the post spacing — usually 8 feet — then add one post at the end.

### How many pickets do I need for a 100 ft fence?

219, with 1×6 pickets. They are really 5.5 inches wide, so it is 2.2 pickets per foot, not 2.

### How much concrete per fence post?

One 80 lb bag, for a 4×4 post in a 10 to 12 inch hole, 24 inches deep.

### How deep should fence posts go?

At least a third of the post goes underground, and below your frost line. 24 inches deep is the usual minimum for a 6 foot fence.

## How much flooring do I need? (https://builditcalculators.com/how-much-flooring-do-i-need.html)

A 12 by 15 foot room takes 198 square feet of flooring with 10% waste — 10 boxes of laminate at 20 square feet a box, or 9 boxes of vinyl plank at 24. Measure the room, add waste, and divide by what is in a box.
### Worked example

A 12 by 15 foot room 180 sq ft

With 10% waste 198 sq ft to order

Laminate, 20 sq ft per box 10 boxes

Vinyl plank, 24 sq ft per box 9 boxes

Underlayment, 100 sq ft per roll 2 rolls

## How the maths works

### Step 1: the room area

Length × width. A 12 by 15 foot room is 180 square feet. Measure each room separately — flooring is ordered by the room, not the house.

### Step 2: add waste

Add 10% for a straight lay in a rectangular room, 15% for a diagonal layout or a room with lots of corners, and 20% for herringbone. The 12 by 15 room needs 198 square feet with 10% waste.

### Step 3: divide by the box size

Laminate is usually about 20 sq ft a box, vinyl plank about 24, hardwood about 20 and engineered hardwood about 22. The exact number is printed on the box. 198 ÷ 20 = 9.9, so 10 boxes of laminate; 198 ÷ 24 = 8.25, so 9 boxes of vinyl plank.

### Underlayment

Allow one roll of underlayment per 100 square feet — 2 rolls for the 12 by 15 room.

### Common room sizes

 | Room   | Area   | With 10% waste   | Laminate boxes   | Vinyl plank boxes

 | 10 × 12 ft   | 120 sq ft   | 132 sq ft   | 7   | 6

 | 12 × 12 ft   | 144 sq ft   | 159 sq ft   | 8   | 7

 | 12 × 15 ft   | 180 sq ft   | 198 sq ft   | 10   | 9

 | 15 × 20 ft   | 300 sq ft   | 330 sq ft   | 17   | 14

## Common questions

### How much flooring do I need for a 12×12 room?

144 square feet, and 159 with 10% waste — 8 boxes of laminate at 20 square feet a box.

### How much extra flooring should I buy?

10% for a straight lay in a rectangular room. Use 15% for diagonal layouts or rooms with lots of corners, and 20% for herringbone.

### How many square feet are in a box of flooring?

It varies by brand — laminate is usually about 20, vinyl plank about 24, hardwood about 20, and engineered hardwood about 22. The exact number is printed on the box.

### How much underlayment do I need?

About one roll per 100 square feet — 2 rolls for a 12 by 15 foot room.

Figures verified November 2026 against supplier listings and several online calculators. These are estimates for planning only — confirm quantities with your supplier before you order.

## How much mulch do I need? (https://builditcalculators.com/how-much-mulch-do-i-need.html)

A 10 by 20 foot bed, 3 inches deep, takes 1.85 cubic yards of mulch — 25 bags of 2 cubic feet. The maths is length × width × depth, divided by 27 to get cubic yards. One cubic yard covers 108 square feet at 3 inches deep.
### Worked example

A 10 by 20 foot bed, 3 inches deep 1.85 cubic yards

In 2 cu ft bags 25 bags

A 10 by 10 foot bed, 3 inches deep 0.93 cubic yards — 13 bags

One cubic yard covers 108 sq ft at 3 in

## How the maths works

### Cubic yards: length × width × depth, divided by 27

A cubic yard is 27 cubic feet. A 10 by 20 foot bed at 3 inches deep is 10 × 20 × (3 ÷ 12) = 50 cubic feet, and 50 ÷ 27 = 1.85 cubic yards.

### Bags: divide by what one bag holds

A 2 cubic foot bag holds 2 cubic feet, so 50 cubic feet ÷ 2 = 25 bags. One cubic yard is 13.5 bags of 2 cubic feet.

### How deep?

Two to three inches for most flower and shrub beds, four inches around trees. More than 4 inches can suffocate roots — and mulch piled against a trunk rots the bark, so keep it a few inches clear of the trunk.

### Coverage at a glance

 | Depth   | One cubic yard covers

 | 2 inches   | 162 sq ft

 | 3 inches   | 108 sq ft

 | 4 inches   | 81 sq ft

## Bulk or bags?

Bags make sense up to about a cubic yard — 13 or 14 bags. Past that, bulk mulch delivered by the yard is usually much cheaper per cubic yard, and you skip hauling dozens of bags home.

## Common questions

### How much mulch do I need for a 100 sq ft bed?

At 3 inches deep, about 0.93 cubic yards — around 13 bags of 2 cubic feet.

### How deep should mulch be?

Two to three inches for most flower and shrub beds, four inches around trees. More than 4 inches can suffocate roots.

### What mulch is best for a hot, dry garden?

Light-coloured bark or straw, 3 to 4 inches deep. It holds moisture and keeps roots cool; gravel can get hot enough to scorch roots.

### How many bags of mulch are in a cubic yard?

13.5 bags of 2 cubic feet.

Figures verified November 2026 against supplier listings and several online calculators. These are estimates for planning only — confirm quantities with your supplier before you order.

## How much paint do I need? (https://builditcalculators.com/how-much-paint-do-i-need.html)

A 12 by 12 foot room with 8 foot ceilings takes 2 gallons of paint for two coats on the walls — 3 gallons if you paint the ceiling too. One gallon covers about 350 square feet per coat, and almost every interior job needs two coats.
### Worked example

A 12 by 12 foot room, 8 foot ceilings 384 sq ft of walls

Minus 1 door and 2 windows 333 sq ft to paint

Two coats 666 sq ft of painting

At 350 sq ft per gallon 1.90 gallons

Buy 2 gallons

With the ceiling too Buy 3 gallons

## How the maths works

### Step 1: the wall area

Add up all four wall lengths and multiply by the ceiling height. A 12 by 12 foot room with 8 foot ceilings has 384 square feet of wall.

### Step 2: subtract doors and windows

Take off about 21 square feet per door (3 × 7 ft) and 15 per window (3 × 5 ft). One door and two windows takes the 12 by 12 room from 384 to 333 square feet.

### Step 3: multiply by the coats, divide by 350

Two coats means 333 × 2 = 666 square feet of painting. At 350 square feet per gallon, that is 1.90 gallons — buy 2 gallons. Add the ceiling (144 sq ft, two coats) and it becomes 3 gallons.

## How many coats?

Two, for almost every interior job. One coat rarely covers evenly — especially over a darker colour, new drywall, or a repair. Primer counts as a coat on bare drywall or stained walls, but it is not a substitute for the second coat of paint.

## Is expensive paint worth it?

Usually yes. Premium paint covers in two coats where economy paint takes three or four, and lasts 10–15 years instead of 2–4. The dearer gallon is often the cheaper job.

## Common questions

### How much paint do I need for a 12×12 room?

333 square feet of wall after doors and windows, two coats is 666 square feet, and at 350 square feet per gallon that is 1.90 gallons — buy 2 gallons, or 3 gallons with the ceiling.

### How many coats of paint do I need?

Two, for almost every interior job. One coat rarely covers evenly.

### How much does a gallon of paint cover?

About 350 square feet per coat on a smooth wall.

### Is expensive paint worth it?

Usually yes. Premium paint covers in two coats where economy paint takes three or four, and lasts 10–15 years instead of 2–4.

Figures verified November 2026 against supplier listings and several online calculators. These are estimates for planning only — confirm quantities with your supplier before you order.

## How much tile do I need? (https://builditcalculators.com/how-much-tile-do-i-need.html)

A 10 by 12 foot room takes 132 twelve-inch tiles — 14 boxes of 10 — with 10% waste built in. Divide the floor area by one tile's area, add waste, and divide by the tiles per box.
### Worked example

A 10 by 12 foot room 120 sq ft

12 × 12 inch tiles 120 tiles

With 10% waste 132 tiles

Boxes of 10 14 boxes

Same room, 12 × 24 inch tiles 66 tiles — 7 boxes

Same room, 6 × 6 inch tiles 480 tiles

## How the maths works

### Step 1: how many tiles

Divide the floor area by one tile's area. A 12×12 inch tile covers 1 square foot, so a 120 square foot room takes 120 tiles. A 12×24 inch tile covers 2 square feet, so the same room takes 60.

### Step 2: add waste

Add 10% for straight rows, 15% for diagonal patterns, herringbone, or rooms with lots of corners. The 10 by 12 room needs 132 twelve-inch tiles with 10% waste.

### Step 3: divide by the box

Divide by the tiles per box and round up. 132 tiles in boxes of 10 is 13.2 — buy 14 boxes.

### Tiles per square foot

 | Tile size   | Area per tile   | Tiles per sq ft

 | 6 × 6 in   | 0.25 sq ft   | 4

 | 12 × 12 in   | 1 sq ft   | 1

 | 12 × 24 in   | 2 sq ft   | 0.5

 | 18 × 18 in   | 2.25 sq ft   | 0.44

## Buy a spare box

Tile dye lots change between batches, and a matching box is hard to find later when one tile cracks. One spare box in the garage is cheap insurance.

## Common questions

### How many tiles do I need?

Divide the floor area by one tile's area — a 12×12 inch tile covers 1 square foot — then add 10% waste.

### How much extra tile should I buy?

10% for straight rows, 15% for diagonal patterns, herringbone, or rooms with lots of corners.

### Should I buy a spare box of tile?

Yes. Tile dye lots change between batches, and a matching box is hard to find later when one tile cracks.

### How many tiles do I need for a 10×12 room?

132 twelve-inch tiles with 10% waste — 14 boxes of 10.

Figures verified November 2026 against supplier listings and several online calculators. These are estimates for planning only — confirm quantities with your supplier before you order.

## How much topsoil or gravel do I need? (https://builditcalculators.com/how-much-topsoil-or-gravel-do-i-need.html)

A 10 by 10 foot area, 6 inches deep, takes 1.85 cubic yards — 1.85 tons of topsoil or 2.59 tons of gravel. Suppliers sell topsoil by the cubic yard and gravel by the ton, so work out the volume first, then convert.
### Worked example

A 10 by 10 foot area, 6 inches deep 1.85 cubic yards

As topsoil 1.85 tons

As gravel 2.59 tons

As sand 2.50 tons

## How the maths works

### Cubic yards: length × width × depth, divided by 27

A 10 by 10 foot area at 6 inches deep is 10 × 10 × (6 ÷ 12) = 50 cubic feet, and 50 ÷ 27 = 1.85 cubic yards.

### Tons: multiply by the weight per yard

Topsoil weighs about 1 ton per cubic yard, gravel about 1.4 tons, and sand about 1.35 tons. So 1.85 cubic yards is 1.85 tons of topsoil, 2.59 tons of gravel, or 2.50 tons of sand.

### Common sizes

 | Area   | Cubic yards   | Tons of gravel

 | 10 × 10 ft at 6 in   | 1.85   | 2.59

 | 10 × 20 ft at 6 in   | 3.70   | 5.19

 | 20 × 20 ft at 4 in   | 4.94   | 6.91

## Which material?

Topsoil for lawns and garden beds. Crusher run (road base) for driveways and paths — it packs down hard, and it is the cheapest gravel at $20–$40 a ton delivered. Pea gravel for paths and drainage at $30–$60 a ton. For vegetables, screened loam with compost mixed in; blueberries are the exception — they need acidic soil, not ordinary topsoil.

## Common questions

### How many tons of gravel are in a cubic yard?

About 1.4 tons.

### Which gravel is cheapest?

Crusher run (road base), about $20–$40 a ton delivered. Pea gravel costs the most, about $30–$60 a ton.

### What soil is best for vegetables?

Screened loam with compost mixed in. Blueberries are the exception — they need acidic soil, not ordinary topsoil.

### How much topsoil do I need for a 10×10 area, 6 inches deep?

1.85 cubic yards — 1.85 tons of topsoil, or 2.59 tons if you are ordering gravel.

Figures verified November 2026 against supplier listings and several online calculators. These are estimates for planning only — confirm quantities with your supplier before you order.

## Power Station Runtime Calculator — How Long Will a Power Station Last? (https://builditcalculators.com/power-station.html)

Power station calculator

# How long will a power station last?

A power station's label says watt-hours, but you only get about 85% of that out — the inverter takes the rest. Tick the devices you would run, say how many hours a day each one runs, and the calculator tells you how many days your station lasts, and how long each device runs on its own.

## Your station and your devices

Battery size (watt-hours)

1024 Wh is a mid-size station (EcoFlow Delta 2). Check the Wh on the station's label or spec sheet.

Devices (tick to include; watts are typical running watts):

 - Phone charger: 10 W, 3 hours a day
 - Laptop: 60 W, 4 hours a day
 - Wi-Fi router: 10 W, 24 hours a day
 - LED light: 10 W, 5 hours a day
 - Small fan: 50 W, 8 hours a day
 - Mini fridge: 60 W, 8 hours a day
 - Full-size fridge: 150 W, 8 hours a day
 - TV: 100 W, 4 hours a day
 - CPAP machine: 40 W, 8 hours a day
 - Microwave: 1000 W, 0.25 hours a day
 - Space heater: 1500 W, 0 hours a day
 - Kettle: 1500 W, 0.1 hours a day

Watts are typical running watts from manufacturer specs. A fridge cycles on and off, so 8 hours a day is the running equivalent, not 8 hours plugged in. Your own devices may differ — check the label.

Below freezing (0°C / 32°F): lithium batteries give up about 20% of their usable capacity in the cold, and most stations will not charge below freezing.

Days of backup you want: 1

## Your station lasts

0.9 days (about 22 hours) for a 1024 Wh station on the example load.

Usable energy: 870 Wh. Your devices use per day: 960 Wh. Station size you need: 1130 Wh.

How long each device runs alone: phone charger 87.0 hours, laptop 14.5 hours, Wi-Fi router 87.0 hours, LED light 87.0 hours, small fan 17.4 hours.

## Worked example

A 1024 Wh station, running a phone, laptop, router, light and fan: 960 Wh per day. Usable energy (85% of the label): 870 Wh. Days of backup: 0.9 days (about 22 hours). Full-size fridge alone: 5.8 hours. Laptop alone: 14.5 hours. Phone alone: 87 hours. Station size needed for 1 day on this load: 1130 Wh.

## How the maths works

### Usable energy: the label minus 15%

A station's watt-hour rating is measured at the battery's own voltage. Running 120 V devices through the inverter loses about 15%, so the energy you can actually use is the label times 0.85. A 1024 Wh station gives 1024 × 0.85 = 870 Wh.

### Daily use: watts × hours, added up

Each device uses its running watts times the hours it runs each day. Phone 10 × 3 = 30 Wh, laptop 60 × 4 = 240 Wh, router 10 × 24 = 240 Wh, light 10 × 5 = 50 Wh, fan 50 × 8 = 400 Wh. Add them up: 30 + 240 + 240 + 50 + 400 = 960 Wh per day.

### Days of backup: usable ÷ daily

Divide the usable energy by the daily use. 870 ÷ 960 = 0.9 days — about 22 hours. If the answer is under a day, your load is too big for the station, or you need a bigger station.

### Station size needed: daily × days ÷ 0.85

Work backwards from the load: daily use times the days you want, divided by 0.85 to cover the inverter loss. 960 × 1 ÷ 0.85 = 1130 Wh for one full day on the example load.

### Common station sizes on the example load (960 Wh per day)

 - 256 Wh: 218 Wh usable, 0.2 days
 - 512 Wh: 435 Wh usable, 0.5 days
 - 1024 Wh: 870 Wh usable, 0.9 days
 - 2048 Wh: 1741 Wh usable, 1.8 days

### Cold weather: take off another 20%

Lithium batteries give up about 20% of their usable capacity below freezing, and most stations will not charge at all below 0°C (32°F). On the example load, a 1024 Wh station in the cold gives 870 × 0.8 = 696 Wh, which lasts 0.7 days instead of 0.9. Keep the station somewhere warm — inside, in the car, or in an insulated bag — and charge it indoors.

## Common questions

### How long will a 1000 Wh power station run a fridge?

About 5 to 6 hours running flat out. A 1000 Wh station gives about 850 Wh of usable energy, and a full-size fridge draws about 150 watts while it runs, so 850 divided by 150 is about 5.7 hours. In real use a fridge cycles on and off, so it stretches to most of a day.

### Why does my power station run out faster than the label says?

Three reasons. First, the inverter takes about 15% — a 1000 Wh station gives about 850 Wh. Second, the Wh on the label is measured at the battery's own voltage; running 120 V devices through the inverter loses a little more. Third, cold weather cuts capacity by about 20% below freezing. The calculator builds the first and third in.

### What size power station do I need for a day without power?

Add up what you would run: watts times hours for each device. Divide the total by 0.85. The example load on this page — phone, laptop, router, light and fan — uses 960 Wh a day, so it needs a station of about 1130 Wh for one full day.

### Can I charge it while I use it?

Most stations allow pass-through charging — you can plug them into the wall or a solar panel while they power your devices. Charging is slower while the station is also running devices, and a few small stations pause charging when the load is heavy. Check your station's manual.

Figures verified November 2026 against manufacturer spec sheets (EcoFlow, Jackery, Bluetti). Typical running watts only — check your own devices' labels. This page is an estimate for planning, not buying advice.
